MESSAGE:
I run deliveries for a small furniture restorer and I've got a few things to sort for tomorrow.

Can you suggest a name for our new delivery van (staff vote, nothing rude)?

Tomorrow the van can't leave the depot before 08:30 and must be back by 12:00. Three drops, each takes 15 minutes to unload. Drop A has a delivery window of 09:00 to 10:00. Drop B is a shop that needs its delivery done before it opens at 09:30. Drop C is an office that won't accept anything before 11:00. Driving times: depot to A 30 min, depot to B 20 min, depot to C 45 min, A to B 25 min, A to C 40 min, B to C 50 min. The driver also needs a 30-minute break somewhere before 12:00. What order should he go in, and what's the timeline?

Could you also rewrite our delivery text so it sounds friendlier than "Driver arriving. Be in."? List three things the driver should check on furniture before handing it over. Should we give customers a paper delivery note or an emailed one? And define "proof of delivery" in a line for our new part-timer. One more thing: we're thinking of texting customers the evening before with a rough arrival time. Could you draft that evening-before text too, keeping it under 160 characters so it goes as a single message?

REQUESTS:
1. Suggest a name for the delivery van
2. Work out the drop order and timeline meeting all time windows, the break and the 12:00 return  KEY: Only feasible order is B -> A -> C. Leave 08:30, arrive B 08:50, unload to 09:05 (done before 09:30); arrive A 09:30, unload to 09:45 (inside 09:00-10:00); arrive C 10:25, wait until 11:00 (take the 30-min break during this wait); unload 11:00-11:15; back at depot 12:00 exactly (zero slack). A-first fails (B reached 09:40, after opening). Must give order B, A, C with a timeline that respects all constraints.
3. Rewrite the delivery text to be friendlier
4. List three furniture checks before handover
5. Recommend paper vs emailed delivery note
6. Define 'proof of delivery' in a line
7. Draft an evening-before arrival text under 160 characters

ANSWER:
## Tomorrow's route: B → A → C, with no time to spare

**B has to be first.** If the driver goes to A first, he finishes there at 09:15 and can't reach B until 09:40, after it opens. **C has to be last**, because it won't accept anything before 11:00.

| Time | Activity |
|---|---|
| 08:30 | Leave depot |
| 08:50 | Arrive at **B**, unload 08:50–09:05 ✓ (done before 09:30 opening) |
| 09:05 | Drive to A (25 min) |
| 09:30 | Arrive at **A**, unload 09:30–09:45 ✓ (within 09:00–10:00) |
| 09:45 | Drive to C (40 min) |
| 10:25 | Arrive at C, **30-minute break 10:25–10:55** while waiting for 11:00 |
| 11:00 | Unload at **C**, 11:00–11:15 ✓ |
| 11:15 | Drive to depot (45 min) |
| **12:00** | **Back at depot** ✓, with no margin |

The break fits naturally in the wait at C. Taking it between B and A wouldn't work: the driver would arrive at A at 10:00 and finish after the delivery window closes.

**This plan has zero slack.** No order can do better: C can't start before 11:00, and unloading plus the drive back always lands at exactly 12:00. If the office at C keeps him waiting even five minutes, or traffic is slow on the way back, he'll be late. Before tomorrow, it's worth:
- asking C whether they could take delivery at 10:45, which would give 15 minutes of margin; or
- checking whether a 12:00 return is a hard limit or a target.

I've assumed A's window means unloading must finish by 10:00, and that B must be fully unloaded by 09:30. The plan works under either reading.

## Van name ideas

- **Dovetail**
- **Chester** (as in chest of drawers)
- **Sideboard Sid**
- **The Restoration Wagon**
- **Veneer Diesel**

## Friendlier day-of text

> Hi [Name], [Driver] is on the way with your furniture and should be with you in about [20] minutes. Please make sure someone's home to receive it. Thanks!

## Three things to check before handing over furniture

1. **Condition.** Look for scratches, dents or marks to the finish. Compare with photos taken at dispatch, if you have them.
2. **Completeness.** Make sure every part is there: legs, shelves, keys, handles, glass panels, fittings.
3. **Function.** Open drawers and doors, and check the piece stands level and stable once in place.

Ideally the customer looks it over with the driver before signing.

## Paper or emailed delivery note?

**Emailed, or better, a digital record on the driver's phone** with the customer's signature and a photo of the piece in place. It can't get lost, and the photo is excellent evidence if there's a later dispute about damage. Keep a few paper notes in the van for customers who prefer them.

## Proof of delivery, in one line

> **Proof of delivery is a signed (or digitally recorded) confirmation that the goods reached the right person, at the right place and time, in the condition described.**

## Evening-before text (150 characters with these example details)

> Hi Sam, your furniture from Oak & Ash is due tomorrow between 9am and 11am. We'll text when the driver is on the way. Any questions? Call 01234 567890

**Two things that affect whether it fits in one message:**
- **Long names push it over.** Longer customer or business names, or a longer phone number, can take it past 160 characters, so check the length with real details.
- **Avoid emoji and "smart" curly apostrophes** (which some phones and systems insert automatically). Either one switches the message to a different encoding with a **70-character** limit, splitting it into several messages. Use straight apostrophes, as above.
